titles.title: Ex vivo evaluation of corneal permeation and irritation potential associated with proparacaine hydrochloride misuse

descriptions.description: Proparacaine hydrochloride is a topical ocular anesthetic widely used in diagnostic procedures. Although generally safe when properly administered, repeated or unsupervised use has been associated with clinically relevant corneal injury. In contexts where access to topical anesthetics is insufficiently controlled, misuse may result in cumulative epithelial damage and vision-threatening complications. Despite clinical reports and experimental evidence of corneal toxicity, quantitative data linking exposure conditions to structural corneal damage under controlled ex vivo settings remain limited, particularly regarding dose-injury relationships at the tissue level. Porcine corneas were mounted in Franz diffusion cells to quantify permeation by UV–Vis spectrophotometry and evaluate corneal histopathological changes. Both pure proparacaine and the commercial 0.5% proparacaine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution (Alcaine®, Alcon) were assessed under therapeutic (2.25 mg/mL), abuse (4.5 mg/mL), and infinite-dose (53.152 mg/mL) conditions. Negative (phosphate-buffered saline) and positive (99.5% ethanol) controls were included for histopathological assessment. ANOVA was applied to permeation data, and histopathological scores were analyzed using non-parametric tests. Proparacaine showed low permeability (9.33 × 10−7 cm/s), with only a small fraction of the applied dose permeating across the cornea during the experimental period. Permeation increased in a concentration- and time-dependent manner. High-dose and infinite-dose exposure conditions resulted in marked epithelial damage, including spongiosis, chromatin condensation, and desquamation, with severity comparable to that induced by ethanol used as a positive control. Differences between formulations were primarily driven by concentration rather than formulation composition, and a correlation was observed between cumulative permeation and the extent of epithelial injury. Proparacaine demonstrates dose-dependent permeation and histopathological changes, emphasizing the risks associated with misuse. The ex vivo model provides relevant and ethically aligned evidence to support ocular hazard assessment through the characterizing of histopathological changes.

titles.title: Stability of posterior corneal curvature after keratorefractive lenticule extraction: replication data and code

descriptions.description: Deidentified data and analysis code that reproduce all analyses, tables and figures of the article "Stability of posterior corneal curvature after keratorefractive lenticule extraction: a retrospective cohort study" (submitted to BMC Ophthalmology). The package contains one row per analysed eye and postoperative visit (6,201 eye-visits; 2,050 eyes of 1,057 patients treated with SmartSight KLEx on the SCHWIND ATOS, Eye Clinic Svjetlost, Zagreb, 2022–2026). It also contains all eligible MS-39 acquisitions of these eyes, used for the calibration-period and repeatability analyses, together with Python analysis scripts, a data dictionary and reference outputs. The data include flags for a tomographer calibration period (October 2024 to February 2025) that biased curvature measurements. Identifiers are repository-specific; there are no names, record numbers or exact dates. Ethics approval: Eye Clinic Svjetlost, KS-KLEx-Reg001.

titles.title: Topical Kojic Acid Liposomes for Alkali-Induced Corneal Injury: Comparative Study of Uncoated vs. Hyaluronic Acid-Coated Formulations in Corneal Epithelial Repair

descriptions.description: Corneal chemical injuries are ocular emergencies that can progress to severe ulceration, scarring, and vision loss. This study evaluated topically delivered kojic acid (KA) an agent known for cell proliferation and anti-inflammatory properties in an alkali-induced corneal injury model. Uncoated liposomes and HA coated liposomes were investigated to deliver KA in the corneal tissue. Small (∼200 nm; SL-KA, SL-KA-HA) and large (∼500 nm; LL-KA, LL-KA-HA) liposomes and HA coated liposomes were formulated. Larger liposomes either coated or uncoated exhibited superior ex vivo corneal retention compared to smaller nanocarriers, with uncoated large liposomes (LL-KA: 0.613 ± 0.02 µg) achieving higher retention than HA-coated liposomes (LL-KA-HA: 0.372 ± 0.04 µg). In a 21-day rabbit model of alkali-induced corneal injury, untreated controls showed persistent inflammation and cellular adhesion, whereas free KA failed to alleviate necrosis. Conversely, LL-KA and LL-KA-HA significantly enhanced structural healing, preserved intact epithelia, and reduced stromal alterations, with superior tissue recovery in the LL-KA group. HA solution controls preserved the epithelium but failed to resolve underlying stromal inflammation. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a marked reduction in NF-κB expression in liposome-treated groups compared to untreated, free KA, or HA controls. Liposomal delivery of KA offers a promising non-surgical therapy for alkali-induced corneal injuries, with uncoated large liposomes emerged better corneal healing.

titles.title: Proteomic analysis of aqueous humor from patients with Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy reveals downregulated expression of HSP60

descriptions.description:
The aim of the study is to identify proteins with differential abundance among aqueous humor (AqH) samples from patients with mild or advanced Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) compared to control subjects.
Proteins were extracted from AqH samples and analyzed by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. A total of 455 proteins were identified across the three groups, of which 285 proteins were shared across all groups at the identification level and 104 were retained after proteomic filtering for quantitative analysis. Statistical analysis revealed that 48 proteins were significantly downregulated in mild, advanced, or both groups compared to controls, while one was upregulated. Functional enrichment analysis was performed on differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) and indicated that the main biological processes were associated with cell energy metabolism and cytoskeleton disorganization, known hallmarks of FECD pathology. Among all these, HSP60 was selected for further validation. Reduced HSP60 expression was confirmed in additional AqH samples and corneal endothelial tissue samples from FECD patients, supporting the proteomics findings. In conclusion, these results suggest that HSP60 is a disease-associated protein in FECD and a candidate for future functional studies, with possible relevance for biomarker discovery and therapeutic exploration.

descriptions.description:
Dataset Name

The official name of this dataset is CCM-Seg (Corneal Confocal Microscopy Segmentation Dataset). We recommend using CCM-Seg when referring to this dataset in publications, presentations, benchmarks, and other academic materials.

Cite the article



Qiao, Q., Cao, J. & Hou, X. An Annotated Corneal Confocal Microscopy Dataset for Nerve Segmentation and Clinical Characterization. Sci Data (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-07418-6


User Guide

The uncompressed dataset consists of two folders and a Microsoft Excel file, named “images”, “annotations”, and “data.xlsx”, respectively. The first two folders contained the original CCM images and their corresponding segmentation masks, each comprising 410 PNG images. Each original image has a corresponding mask with an identical filename. The “re-annotations” folder includes 10 images selected from each of Set1 and Set2, which were re-annotated by Annotator 2 and Researcher 2.

The filenames are prefixed with a five-digit code following the SPPII pattern: the first digit (S) indicates the set number (1 or 2); the second and third digits (PP) represent the participant number within the set, padded with a leading zero if necessary; and the fourth and fifth digits (II) denote the image number for that participant, also zero-padded when needed. For example, “25104.png” refers to the fourth image (04) of Participant 51 in Set2.

Clinical and demographic information are organised in the Excel file “data.xlsx”, which comprises two distinct sheets. The “Subjects” sheet details information at the subject level, whereas the “Images” sheet provides data at the image level, enabling direct mapping between images and their corresponding clinical data. titles.title: Two-year clinical follow-up data of keratoconus patients fitted with a new large-diameter rigid corneal gas-permeable contact lens

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains clinical and patient-reported data collected during a two-year prospective follow-up of patients with keratoconus fitted with a customized large-diameter rigid corneal gas-permeable contact lens. The dataset includes demographic information, contact lens parameters, corneal and keratoconus-related characteristics, visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, ocular physiology, contact lens wearing time, and patient satisfaction.

The data were collected at baseline and during follow-up visits at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months. The dataset provides longitudinal clinical data from participants who completed the two-year follow-up and is intended to support the reproducibility of the associated research and further research on contact lens fitting and clinical outcomes in keratoconus.

titles.title: Beyond corneal structure in Noonan syndrome: topographic, tomographic, and optical findings

descriptions.description: This study aimed to evaluate corneal topographic, tomographic, and wavefront characteristics in individuals with Noonan syndrome (NS) and to compare these findings with those of healthy controls. This prospective, case–control study included 18 patients with NS (36 eyes) and 19 age- and sex-matched controls (38 eyes). All participants underwent anterior segment tomography and corneal wavefront analysis. Both eyes were included in the analysis, and inter-eye correlation was addressed using generalized estimating equation (GEE) models. Keratometric values, central corneal thickness, and anterior and posterior corneal elevation parameters were comparable between groups (all p > 0.05). Cylindrical refractive error was greater in the NS group (−0.92 ± 0.19 vs − 0.41 ± 0.12 D; p = 0.022). Corneal wavefront analysis demonstrated significantly higher total corneal high-order aberration root mean square (HOA RMS) (0.54 ± 0.03 vs 0.44 ± 0.03 μm; p = 0.004), coma RMS (0.37 ± 0.01 vs 0.27 ± 0.03 μm; p = 0.001), and trefoil RMS (0.27 ± 0.03 vs 0.19 ± 0.02 μm; p = 0.012) in the NS group. Individuals with NS demonstrated preserved corneal structure but exhibited heterogeneous alterations in corneal optical quality, characterized by increased asymmetric high-order aberrations and greater cylindrical refractive error in a subset of patients. These findings suggest variable and predominantly subclinical corneal involvement rather than a uniform ectatic phenotype.

titles.title: Younger Age-Related Incidence of Corneal Limbitis Following Pterygium Excision Combined with Conjunctival-Limbal Autograft

descriptions.description: To investigate the incidence, clinical characteristics, and risk factors of corneal limbitis following pterygium excision with conjunctival-limbal autograft. This retrospective study included 63 eyes of 61 patients with primary nasal pterygium who underwent pterygium excision with conjunctival-limbal autograft. Patients were assessed perioperatively using anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (AS SS-OCT; Anterion, Heidelberg, Germany), and postoperative complications were evaluated during follow-up. Risk factors for corneal limbitis, including age and preoperative AS SS-OCT-guided morphological and optical parameters, were analyzed. Corneal limbitis occurred in 12 of 63 eyes (19.0%), with a mean onset of 19.1 ± 10.9 weeks postoperatively. Eyes with limbitis were significantly younger than those without (45.3 ± 8.1 vs. 60.5 ± 9.5 years, p < 0.001), while other demographic, clinical severity, and morphological parameters were not significantly different between the two groups. On multivariate logistic regression analysis, younger age was the only independent risk factor for postoperative corneal limbitis (p = 0.007, OR = 0.674). ROC curve analysis identified a cutoff age of 49.5 years (AUC = 0.895, sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 83.3%). The incidence of corneal limbitis was significantly higher in patients younger than 50 years (10/14 eyes, 71.4%) than in those aged 50 years or older (2/49 eyes, 4.1%) (p < 0.001). All limbitis cases resolved with anti-inflammatory treatment. Corneal limbitis may represent a notable postoperative complication following pterygium excision with conjunctival-limbal autograft, occurring predominantly in younger patients. Younger age appeared to be associated with a higher risk, although this finding requires validation in larger cohorts.

titles.title: Supplemental Material for: Topical Losartan in the Management of Corneal Scarring from Trauma and Infection: A Case Series

descriptions.description: Introduction:Losartan inhibits ERK-mediated signaling in the noncanonical transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) pathway, which may play a role in corneal fibrosis. Rabbit studies have shown that topical losartan can reduce stromal scarring, fibrosis, and myofibroblast formation after corneal injuries and other clinical insults. Its use in humans has since been reported for corneal scarring and haze following LASIK, corneal cross-linking, and herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus infections. Here, we present several additional clinical scenarios in which topical losartan has demonstrated potential efficacy in reducing corneal scarring. Case Presentations:Cases which improved with topical losartan included a full thickness corneal laceration from an open globe injury, four cases of Pseudomonas contact-lens related corneal ulcers, one case of a likely herpetic-related corneal ulcer, and one case of a full-thickness Fusarium fungal ulcer. Topical losartan was initiated between two weeks to over ten months after the initial corneal insult, with most patients starting treatment within one to two months of presentation. No patients experienced any significant side effects from topical losartan use.Conclusions: Topical losartan may be an effective treatment for corneal scarring secondary to trauma or infection either following or in conjunction with corticosteroid therapy. Patients with such scarring should be considered for inclusion in future clinical trialswhich investigatethe efficacy and safety of topical losartan treatment.

titles.title: Demonstration set of CTL-GAN-generated synthetic fluorescein corneal images for dry eye disease grading (Oxford scale, 100 images per grade)

descriptions.description:
This demonstration dataset contains de-identified synthetic anterior segment (fluorescein-stained corneal) images for dry eye disease grading on the Oxford scale (Grade 0–5), generated using the collaborative transfer learning with generative adversarial networks (CTL-GAN) framework. It comprises two sets corresponding to the two source institutions in the study, Samsung Medical Center (SMC) and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU).

SMC dataset: synthetic images generated by a StyleGAN3 generator trained directly on the internal SMC cohort of real fluorescein-stained images.

SYSU dataset: synthetic images generated from SYSU data using CTL-GAN. The generator weights by the SMC dataset were transferred and adapted to the small SYSU dataset without exchanging any raw images, simulating an institution with limited data benefiting from a pretrained generator.

Each set provides 100 synthetic images per Oxford grade, organized into one folder per source and grade. This is a representative subset provided for demonstration and reproducibility, not the full set used for model training. All images are machine-generated; no real patient images are included. Full methodology and evaluation are described in the associated publication.

titles.title: Toward clinically relevant automated corneal biomanufacturing with human-derived FBS alternatives [data]

affiliation: ZMBH - Center for Molecular Biology of Heidelberg University
contributors.name: Taoum, Alexandre

descriptions.description: The replacement of animal-derived components from cell culture protocols is essential for the development of human-compatible and clinically translatable systems. Fetal bovine serum (FBS) is still widely used for cell expansion, although its xenogeneic origin and batch variability limit regulatory compliance. In this study, human platelet lysate (hPL) and human serum (HS) were assessed as low-serum (2%) alternatives to FBS during the subculture phase of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSC) prior to keratocyte differentiation for corneal tissue engineering. BM-MSC were gradually adapted over four days to 2% FBS, hPL, or HS, maintained for seven days, and then transferred to serum-free keratocyte differentiation medium for 14 days in either two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) cultures in 30 wt% riboflavin-arginine-triggered gelatin methacryloyl (RA-GelMA) hydrogels crosslinked under visible blue light. To demonstrate the applicability of this approach in corneal tissue engineering, differentiation was evaluated by immunofluorescence and quantitative PCR in 2D cultures, and by immunofluorescence in 3D cultures. Both hPL and HS maintained metabolic activity, supported keratocyte-associated marker expression, and suppressed α-SMA, performing comparably to FBS, thereby supporting their use as clinically compliant, human-derived alternatives for xeno-reduced corneal biomanufacturing.

titles.title: A novel ZEB1 splice-site variant causing early-onset type 3 posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy and suspected corneal ectasia

descriptions.description: Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy type 3 (PPCD3) is an autosomal dominant endothelial dystrophy caused by variations in the ZEB1 gene. We report a pediatric case presenting with progressive visual impairment associated with simultaneous features of corneal ectasia and endothelial dystrophy. A 9-year-old boy presented with progressive diminution of vision and high myopia. Slit-lamp examination revealed prominent corneal nerves, and central corneal steepening, along with diffuse endothelial guttae and a beaten-metal appearance of the endothelium. Multimodal imaging including Scheimpflug tomography that demonstrated marked bilateral corneal steepening with tomographic features suggestive of corneal ectasia (Kmax 59.0 D in the right eye and 61.6 D in the left eye). Interestingly, central corneal thickness was increased (636 µm in the right eye and 659 µm in the left eye), feature atypical of keratoconus. Specular microscopy demonstrated reduced endothelial cell density. Whole-exome sequencing of the proband identified a novel heterozygous splice-site variant in ZEB1 (chr10:g.31510671A > T; c.485-2A > T), affecting the canonical 3′ splice acceptor site. Targeted next-generation sequencing of parental blood samples confirmed the variant in the father (heterozygous) and its absence in mother, consistent with paternal inheritance. This case provides additional evidence supporting the recognized association between ZEB1-related PPCD3 and suspected corneal ectasia, while describing a novel splice-site ZEB1 variant.

titles.title: Supplemental Material for: A Biomechanically Guided Multimodal Surgical Strategy for Cataract Surgery in an Eye With Extreme Corneal Thinning After Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis: A Case Report

descriptions.description: IntroductionCataract surgery in eyes with extreme corneal thinning secondary to toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is technically challenging because of marked structural fragility and ocular surface instability. We report a multimodal surgical strategy that facilitated safe completion of cataract surgery in such a high-risk eye.Case PresentationAn 80-year-old woman with a history of TEN presented with visually significant cataract in the right eye. She had severe localized corneal thinning with a minimum corneal thickness of 138 μm and a history of corneal perforation approximately 10 years earlier. Reliable keratometric measurements were not possible because of marked corneal irregularity, and anterior segment optical coherence tomography was used for structural assessment. Cataract surgery was performed using a combination of heads-up three-dimensional visualization with monochrome filtering, a transconjunctival single-plane sclerocorneal incision, dispersive ophthalmic viscosurgical device protection, external corneal support with a disposable diagnostic contact lens, and low intraoperative intraocular pressure (20–30 mmHg) maintained with active fluidics. The procedure was completed without intraoperative complications, and visual acuity improved from 0.04 to 0.10 (decimal) at 1 week postoperatively, with a stable corneal appearance. According to follow-up information obtained from the referring ophthalmologist, a delayed corneal perforation subsequently occurred at the site of pre-existing thinning approximately two months after surgery and was managed with a therapeutic soft contact lens; visual acuity had further improved to 0.30 at last available follow-up.ConclusionA biomechanically guided multimodal surgical strategy combining enhanced visualization, ocular surface protection, external corneal support, a transconjunctival single-planesclerocorneal incision, and controlled low intraoperative intraocular pressure may facilitate safe completion of cataract surgery in carefully selected eyes with extreme corneal thinning. This case highlights the potential value of minimizing and redistributing both externally and internally generated mechanical stress as a practical surgical framework for such eyes, although the underlying corneal structural fragility itself may not be resolved by cataract surgery alone.

titles.title: Visual and Refractive Outcomes of Corneal Refractive Surgery for Hyperopic and Mixed Astigmatism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

descriptions.description: To evaluate the visual and refractive outcomes of corneal refractive surgery (PRK, LASIK, and SMILE) for hyperopic and mixed astigmatism. The clinical question addressed was: in adults with hyperopic or mixed astigmatism, how effective and safe are modern corneal refractive procedures, without alternative surgical comparators, in reducing refractive cylinder and improving uncorrected distance visual acuity? Hyperopic and mixed astigmatism are less predictable to correct than myopic errors due to biomechanical and ablation-profile complexity. Historically, these treatments showed higher regression and retreatment rates. With advances in excimer and femtosecond platforms, updated evidence is needed to inform clinical decision-making and patient counseling regarding expected efficacy, predictability, and safety. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA 2020 and Cochrane guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from January 2010 to March 2025. Eligible studies included prospective, retrospective, or randomized human studies evaluating PRK, LASIK, or SMILE for hyperopic or mixed astigmatism. Case reports, small series (<10 eyes), intraocular procedures, and presbyopia treatments were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Case Series Studies. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed, and heterogeneity was quantified with I<sup>2</sup> statistics. Twenty-three studies (3,561 eyes) were included. Mean preoperative cylinder was 2.45 ± 1.23 D. Pooled residual astigmatism was 0.47 D (95% CI, 0.04–0.90) for hyperopic and 0.67 D (95% CI, 0.37–0.97) for mixed astigmatism. Approximately 66% (hyperopic) and 50% (mixed) achieved ≤ 0.50 D residual cylinder; 81% and 83%, respectively, were within ≤ 1.00 D. Uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) of 20/20 or better was achieved in 60% (hyperopic) and 63% (mixed). Loss of ≥1 line of corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) occurred in 6% (95% CI, 0.01–0.14) of hyperopic and 5% (95% CI, 0.03–0.15) of mixed eyes (pooled random-effects estimates). No significant differences were found between groups in comparative meta-analysis. Modern corneal refractive surgery provides substantial cylinder reduction, high predictability, and excellent safety in hyperopic and mixed astigmatism. Although heterogeneity and predominantly non-randomized designs limit certainty, current laser technologies achieve clinically meaningful outcomes comparable between groups, supporting their use in appropriately selected patients.

titles.title: A Risk Prediction Model for Normal-Tension Glaucoma Progression Integrating Genetic Markers and Corneal Biomechanics

descriptions.description: Normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) is characterized by progressive optic nerve damage despite intraocular pressure remaining consistently within the normal range. Predicting disease progression in patients with confirmed NTG remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model integrating genetic risk scores and corneal biomechanical parameters to predict progression risk in patients with NTG, identify independent predictors, and quantify the contribution of individual features to support precision clinical management. A total of 342 patients with NTG were consecutively enrolled at a tertiary hospital and randomly allocated to training set (n = 238) and validation set (n = 104) at a ratio of 7:3. Baseline characteristics and six core indicators were collected. Candidate predictors were selected through univariate analysis and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with 10-fold cross-validation and the λ-1se criterion. Independent predictors were subsequently identified using multivariable logistic regression. Three machine learning models—random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and logistic regression (LR)—were developed. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to interpret feature contributions. Univariate analysis revealed significant differences in all six indicators between the progression and non-progression groups (p < .05). Multivariable logistic regression further confirmed that all six indicators were independently associated with NTG progression (p < .05). The RF model demonstrated the best predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.760 (95% confidence interval (CI) : 0.678–0.842) in the training set and 0.747 (95% CI: 0.623–0.871) in the validation set. It outperformed both the SVM model (training AUC = 0.704; validation AUC = 0.694) and the LR model (training AUC = 0.742; validation AUC = 0.729). SHAP analysis ranked the features, in descending order of contribution, as mean retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL) thickness, first applanation velocity, visual field mean deviation, relative tear GNAI1 level, polygenic risk score for NTG, and relative tear PRDX4 level. The calibration curves showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, while DCA demonstrated a high clinical net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. A model integrating corneal biomechanical parameters, genetic risk scores, and tear molecular biomarkers was developed to predict the risk of NTG progression and demonstrated potential clinical utility. This model may provide a quantitative reference for risk stratification and personalised management in patients with NTG.

descriptions.description: This dataset contains experimental and finite element simulation data generated to investigate the rate-dependent mechanical behavior of the human cornea under uniaxial tensile loading and Corneal Visualization Scheimpflug Technology (Corvis ST) air-puff loading. Human corneal stromal lenticules were obtained from 20 patients who underwent small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) surgery at ShanXi Aier Eye Hospital, Taiyuan, China. A total of 40 corneal lenticules were collected, from which 80 superior–inferior strip specimens were prepared. The specimens were allocated to four strain-rate groups, with 20 specimens per group, and subjected to uniaxial tensile testing at strain rates of 0.001, 0.1, 0.5, and 1 s-1. Nominal stress was calculated from the measured tensile force and estimated undeformed cross-sectional area, while axial strain was determined using digital image correlation.Preoperative Corvis ST examinations were performed in both eyes of the 20 participants, yielding 40 recordings. Frame-by-frame deflection-amplitude (DA) data were used to calculate the mean DA waveform and corresponding standard deviation. The experimental tensile and Corvis ST data were further combined with a fiber-reinforced viscoelastic constitutive model and whole-eye finite element simulations to characterize corneal deformation under transient air-puff loading.The dataset provides source data supporting the quantitative results presented in the associated study, including mean and standard deviation of nominal stress–strain responses at four strain rates, experimental Corvis ST DA data, best-fit and comparison finite element DA curves, stored-energy components and their relative contributions during air-puff loading, the load-bearing fiber activation factor, and DA curves obtained from the full and reduced viscoelastic models. These data support the evaluation of matrix–fiber mechanical interactions, rate-dependent viscoelasticity, and the contribution of equilibrium and non-equilibrium constitutive branches to corneal deformation during Corvis ST testing.

titles.title: MassIVE MSV000102500 - ARTmax Associated Tear Proteome

Keratoconus is a progressive heterogeneous corneal ectatic disorder characterized by focal stromal thinning and anterior protrusion leading to irregular astigmatism, myopia, and higher-order aberrations that impair visual quality. In advanced stages, corneal scarring may further compromise vision. Diagnosis currently relies on corneal imaging modalities capable of detecting structural alterations, including anterior and posterior surface elevation changes, localized steepening, and progressive stromal thinning. Nevertheless, alterations do not necessarily occur simultaneously, complicating both early detection and the objective definition of disease progression. Despite efforts to standardize progression criteria, no universal consensus exists. Current recommendations advocate defining progression using consistent changes across multiple tomographic parameters rather than relying on a single measurement, although quantitative thresholds remain heterogeneous across studies. Composite indices, such as the Belin Ambrosio D value, and the evaluation of multiple tomographic parameters have been proposed to improve sensitivity and specificity compared with single metrics such as maximum keratometry or minimal pachymetry. However, the absence of unified progression thresholds increases the risk of delayed intervention or overtreatment, underscoring the need for objective biomarkers that reflect underlying biological activity rather than solely geometric change.
MassIVE MSV000102482 - Labeled quantitative (TMT) proteomics of normal human primary trabecular meshwork cells

The trabecular meshwork (TM) is a filter-like tissue in the conventional aqueous humor outflow pathway of the anterior eye chamber, critically involved in regulating intraocular pressure (IOP). TM dysfunction is associated with primary open angle glaucoma (POAG), a leading cause of irreversible blindness. This labeled quantitative proteomics (TMT) dataset was collected from 18 normal (non-glaucomatous) human primary TM cell strains contributed by seven laboratories across the US and UK (the TM omics consortium: labs of Drs. Kate Keller, Samuel Herberg, Yiqin Du, Dona Peters, Padmanabhan Pattabiraman, and Anh Pham from the US, and Dr. Carl Sheridan from the UK). TM cells were isolated from human cadaver eyes procured from local eye banks or from deidentified corneal rims obtained after surgical procedures. Institutional Review Boards from each contributing lab confirmed that use of cadaveric tissue does not constitute research involving human subjects. All studies adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. The 18 strains derived from 7 female and 11 male donors, spanning three age groups: under 40, 40 to 60, and over 60 years. Cells were cultured between passages 3 and 5. Approximately 300,000 to 400,000 cells per tube were pelleted by centrifugation and stored at negative 80 degrees Celsius prior to shipment to the Dr. Sanjoy K. Bhattacharya laboratory at Miami Integrative Metabolomic Research Center (MIMRC) for multiomic analyses. The following TMT labels: 126, 127N, 127C, 128N, 128C, 129N, 129C, 130N, 130C, 131N, 131C, 132N, 132C, 133N, 133C, 134N, 134C, 135N tagged these sample names supplied by individual labs: 2018_1233, 2020_0984, 2022_1149, 2021_1493, HTM 14, HTM 19, HTM 36, TM 165, TM 214, TM 181, #2354, #2355, HTM L_3, HTM L_4, 231011, 2396E, NH 5034, 2396D. For analysis, samples were renamed MC1 to MC18 (Metabolomic Center), linked to original lab names and sample numbers in MIMRC internal records. Protein extraction used the EasyPep Magnetic MS Sample Prep Kit, 96 reactions (cat. no. A57867, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) per manufacturer recommendations. Three synthetic peptide standards (Regen III: LLO, SEB, CFP) were spiked in at 36 uM each during extraction to measure extraction efficiency. Protein amounts were estimated by dot blot densitometry and ImageJ, normalized to 50 ug/mL across all samples. All samples were labeled using an 18plex TMTpro (cat. no. A52045, Thermo Fisher Scientific) kit for unique isobaric tags. After quenching, labels were pooled and dried via CentriVap Vacuum Concentrator (cat. no. 7810014, LABCONCO, Kansas City, MO). Before analysis, dried samples were reconstituted in 48 uL of 2% acetonitrile in water with 0.1% formic acid. Two post-extraction Regen II human peptide standards (A1315 and HH4B) containing isobaric 13C and 15N labels were spiked at 54 uM each as ionization controls, then sonicated in an ultrasonic water bath for 15 min for total solubilization. Samples were transferred to autosampler vials. Untargeted LC MS/MS was performed on a Thermo Scientific Vanquish Neo UHPLC System coupled to a QExactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were ionized and detected using an EASY Spray HPLC Column (cat. no. ES900, 150 mm 75 um 3 um) coupled to an EASYSpray Source (cat. no. ES081), and 1 uL was injected. Flow rate was 0.300 uL/min. Mobile phase A was water with 0.1% formic acid (v/v); phase B was 80% acetonitrile in water with 0.1% formic acid (v/v). Column temperature was 55 degrees Celsius. Spray voltage was 1.92 kV, capillary temperature 300 degrees Celsius, S Lens RF level 60.0. For full scans: mass range 375 to 1400 m/z, resolution 70,000, 1 microscan, AGC target 3 times 106, maximum injection time 50 ms. For ddMS2: mass range 200 to 2000 m/z, resolution 35,000, AGC target 1 times 105, maximum injection time 100 ms. Instrument set to Top 10, isolation window 1.2 m/z, NCE 32. Intensity threshold was 2.04 times 104, dynamic exclusion 30.0 s. Raw data were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer 3.0 with a Sequest HT search engine. The human proteome (SwissProt + TrEMBL, UniProt) was the target database. Maximum missed cleavage sites were 2, minimum peptide length 6. Precursor mass tolerance was 10 ppm, fragment mass tolerance 0.02 Da. Post-translational modifications included oxidation, acetylation, carbamidomethylation, and TMTpro. Normalization was to total peptide amount. Submitted raw data includes peptides identified at high, medium, and low confidence levels, enabling future user-defined filtrations. Target FDR was applied: 0.01 (strict) and 0.05 (relaxed). An 18plex TMT label reagent kit was used as the quantification method.
Supplementary Material for: Robotic Assisted-Intravitreous Light Pipe Illumination for Cataract Surgery in Eyes with Corneal Opacity: Case Reports

descriptions.description:
Introduction: In cataract surgery for eyes with corneal opacity, reduced intraoperative visibility remains a major surgical challenge. To enhance intraoperative visualization, OQrimo, a robotic medical device approved in Japan, was used to hold a light guide. Outcomes of three eyes from two cases are reported.
Case Presentation: Case 1: A 48-year-old man developed bilateral corneal opacity from graft-versus-host disease following umbilical cord blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia. At age 45, he underwent penetrating keratoplasty in the right eye but declined surgery in the left eye. Bilateral cataract surgery under general anesthesia was performed. Due to poor visibility under the surgical microscope in both eyes, a 25-gauge light pipe was inserted into the vitreous cavity and stabilized using OQrimo, thereby improving intraoperative visibility and enabling successful cataract surgery in both eyes.
Case 2: A 74-year-old man had previously undergone pterygium excision with conjunctival autograft transplantation for a lesion involving the pupillary area of the left eye. Residual central corneal opacity remained, and cataract surgery was performed six months later. Due to poor microscopic visibility, a 25-gauge light pipe was inserted into the vitreous cavity and held using OQrimo. While visualization improved, the weight of the OQrimo arm caused ocular deviation, preventing stable positioning and necessitating its discontinuation.
Conclusions: OQrimo effectively enhanced intraoperative visibility in cataract surgery for eyes with corneal opacity, although stable positioning was occasionally challenging.

titles.title: MassIVE MSV000102028 - Proteomic characterization of ocular tear fluid reveals preclinical biomarkers of sulfur mustard toxicity

Sulfur mustard (SM) vapor causes ocular injury after a 6-24 h latent period, when molecular damage has occurred, but clinical signs are not yet apparent. Characterizing ocular responses during this early phase is important for understanding SM pathogenesis, identifying molecular readouts of injury progression, and developing biomarkers of exposure. Tear fluid is well-suited for this purpose because it can be collected noninvasively and reflects responses from injured ocular tissues. We tested whether temporal changes in the tear fluid proteome reflect cellular and molecular responses to corneal SM exposure. Rabbits were exposed to SM vapor using a corneal vapor cap, and tear fluid was collected at baseline, 4 h, 1 d, and 5 d, corresponding to the latent period, acute lesion, and early recovery. A large proteomic response was detected at 4 h, before clinical signs emerged, involving extracellular injury signaling, epithelial injury, and innate immune activation. By 1 d, the tear fluid proteome transitioned to inflammatory cell activation with metabolic, redox, and proteostasis stress. By 5 d, the response was reduced but retained a residual signature of immune, epithelial, and stress responses. This temporal progression is consistent with the molecular mechanisms of SM toxicity and provides insight into acute ocular vesicant injury. These findings establish tear fluid as a noninvasive molecular reporter of ocular SM injury progression. They also reveal a molecular signature of vesicant exposure, which emerges prior to clinical signs, and provide foundational data for developing tear-based biomarkers of chemical exposure, injury assessment, and therapeutic testing.

Permanent Senescence Via p16 Leads to Guttae Formation in an In Vitro Human Corneal Endothelial Cell Model

descriptions.description:
Purpose: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) is characterized by corneal endothelial cell (CEnC) degeneration and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. FECD is an age-related disorder manifested by upregulation of senescence markers. However, the association between senescence and pathological ECM accumulation remains unclear. This study investigated whether senescence mediated cell-cycle arrest drives aberrant ECM deposition and guttae formation in FECD.

Methods: A chronic stress (CS) model was established by concurrently exposing immortalized human CEnCs to ultraviolet-A light (UVA; 25 J/cm2) and 4-hydroxyestradiol (4OHE2; 20 µM) on days 1, 6, and 21, followed by approximately a 60-day recovery period. In vitro guttae were characterized using brightfield microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), immunofluorescence, and compared with FECD specimens. Cell cycle dynamics, senescence markers, and ECM expression were assessed using flow-cytometry, cell sorting, immunostaining, ELISA, and RT-PCR.

Results: In vitro guttae displayed characteristic morphology and ultrastructural similarity to FECD guttae. CS-exposed CEnCs showed significant CDKN2A upregulation (42-fold, P < 0.01) and increased p16 positivity (63 ± 12% vs. 7 ± 3% in controls, P < 0.0001), indicating senescence. Flow cytometry revealed accumulation of CS cells in G0/G1 (74 ± 6% vs. 57 ± 3%, P < 0.0001) phase. G0/G1 sorted p16+ cells exhibited upregulation of COL4A1 (188-fold, P < 0.0001) and LAMB1 (98-fold, P < 0.05). Immunostaining confirmed p16 colocalization with COL4A1 and LAMB1 in CS cells and FECD tissues. ELISA showed elevated levels of TGFBIp in the conditioned media obtained from CS-exposed cells.

Conclusions: G0/G1-arrested p16+ve senescent CEnCs promote pathological ECM deposition and guttae formation. This model, integrating environmental, hormonal, and aging factors, provides a biologically relevant platform for studying FECD and testing therapeutics.

titles.title: p16-mediated G0/G1 cell cycle arrest leads to SASP and fibrosis in Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy

descriptions.description: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) is an age-related disorder characterized by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and loss of corneal endothelial cells (CEnCs), eventually leading to corneal blindness. Despite known environmental and genetic contributors, the roles of aging and hormonal influences, particularly in the predominantly female population, remain underexplored in FECD. This study investigates the impact of chronic exposure to combined ultra-violet (UV-A) light and the oxidized estrogen metabolite 4-hydroxyestradiol (4-OHE2) on healthy CEnCs, primarily focusing on the cellular senescence pathway implicated in FECD pathogenesis. Our results show that prolonged exposure triggers G0/G1 cell cycle arrest through the p16-pRB pathway, inducing a senescence-mediated pro-secretory phenotype. The senescent cells in G0/G1 phase concurrently upregulated the fibrotic and extracellular matrix (ECM) markers indicating a complex relationship between senescence with fibrosis and ECM deposition. Additionally, multiplex analysis to detect senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) after chronic exposure revealed significant upregulation of pathogenic factors such as IL-8 and IL-17, which were attenuated by SB225002 (anti-CXCR2) and secukinumab (anti-IL-17A). Senolytic cocktail of Dasatinib and Quercetin treatment alleviated fibrosis by selectively eliminating senescent cells and improved the survival of healthy cells. This study introduces a novel in vitro model of FECD, revealing the crucial role of cell cycle modulation, senescence and interleukins in the disease advancement and pathogenesis. The findings suggest that targeting senescence and cytokine-driven inflammation could be a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating FECD progression.

titles.title: Supplementary Material for: Longitudinal change in corneal curvature and Fourier indices after corneal suture removal in corneal lacerations

descriptions.description:
Introduction: The purpose of this study is to investigate the longitudinal changes in corneal curvature and refractive components after suture removal in full-thickness corneal laceration using Swept Source Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (SS AS-OCT).
Methods: Thirty patients were included in this study. The patients were divided into three groups according to the location of the wound on the cornea: central, paracentral and peripheral. SS AS-OCT was performed before corneal suture removal, 1 hour, 1 week and 2 weeks after corneal suture removal. The corneal curvature parameters and Fourier indices were compared longitudinally in each group.
Results: After removing the corneal suture, the changes in aveK and spherical component were mostly in the first week, and less than 0.25D in the second week except the spherical component in the central group. The cylinder, regular astigmatism, asymmetry, and higher-order irregularity decreased after suture removal. The patterns of change in the refractive components differ a little with different location of the wound. The best-corrected visual acuity improved after suture removal in all groups. 
Conclusions: The current study demonstrates the changes in corneal curvature and refractive components after corneal suture removal in various locations of corneal laceration. This information provides a reference for deciding the time and strategy of subsequent procedures for visual rehabilitation.

titles.title: A Multi-Parameter Corneal Tomography Dataset for Machine Learning–Driven IOL Selection and Corneal Subtype Classification

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains Pentacam-derived corneal tomographic and biometric parameters collected from 61 eyes of patients undergoing preoperative assessment for cataract surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation. The data were acquired using a standardized Scheimpflug tomography protocol with the Pentacam HR system.

Each record represents a single eye and includes 35 variables encompassing anterior and posterior corneal curvature (K1, K2, KMAX), astigmatism magnitude and axis, corneal asphericity (Q-value), Total Corneal Refractive Power (TCRP), higher-order aberrations (HOA), spherical aberration (Z4,0), the Belin/Ambrósio Deviation index (BAD-D), wavefront root-mean-square (RMS) metrics, central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber parameters, white-to-white distance (HWTW), corneal volume, axial length, refractive error classification, pupil diameter, and selected IOL type.

Eyes are clinically classified into six corneal subtypes:

Normal
High spherical aberration
Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy
High higher-order aberrations
Combined high HOA and high SA
High HOA with corneal ectasia

The dataset is provided as a structured Excel file (.xlsx) with one row per eye and one column per parameter. A companion parameter glossary document (.docx) defines all variables, units, and normative reference ranges.
